column1: What are the two dominant 8-bit CPU architectures used in retro consoles, and what core design philosophy distinguishes them?
column2: MOS 6502 (simple, orthogonal instruction set, pushes complexity to programmer, cheap) vs. Zilog Z80 (richer instruction set, extra register banks, built-in DRAM refresh, more self-sufficient but heavier silicon).

column1: Which processor family powered the NES, and what was its specific chip variant?
column2: The 6502 family, via the Ricoh 2A03, a near-identical clone of the MOS 6502 with integrated audio hardware.

column1: What 16-bit CPU did the SNES use, and what architecture was it extended from?
column2: The 65C816, a 16-bit extension of the original 6502 architecture.

column1: Why couldn't the NES's 6502 CPU directly generate video output by writing pixel data each frame?
column2: A 256×240 frame at 60Hz requires ~3,686,400 pixel decisions/sec, but the 1.79MHz 6502 only executes ~500,000 useful instructions/sec—an order of magnitude short. Dedicated PPU silicon offloads raster generation in parallel with the CPU.

column1: How much work RAM and VRAM did the original NES ship with?
column2: 2 KB of work RAM and 2 KB of video RAM.

column1: Why did cartridge-based systems invert the traditional ROM/RAM execution model?
column2: Cartridges memory-mapped ROM directly into the processor's address space, enabling instant random access and eliminating load times—unlike disk-based systems that must load software into RAM before execution.

column1: What is palette indirection in retro graphics hardware, and why was it necessary?
column2: Tile/sprite pixel data stores small indices (2–4 bits) into palette RAM rather than full RGB values, conserving the limited kilobytes of VRAM available on these systems.

column1: How many simultaneous on-screen colors could the NES display, and from how large a master palette?
column2: 25 simultaneous colors (16 background + 16 sprite entries, with overlap) from a 64-color master palette.

column1: What raster-scan parameters govern NTSC composite video timing on retro consoles?
column2: ~15.7 kHz horizontal scan rate, 262.5 scanlines per frame, with the electron beam sweeping left-to-right then retracing vertically during the vertical blank interval.

column1: What distinguishes PSG (Programmable Sound Generator) audio synthesis from FM synthesis in retro sound chips?
column2: PSGs (e.g., NES 2A03, SN76489) generate sound via direct waveform lookup tables or hard-wired oscillators producing simple waves (pulse, triangle, noise). FM synthesis chips (e.g., Genesis YM2612) generate complex timbres by modulating oscillator frequencies against each other.

column1: What four duty cycle settings did the NES 2A03's pulse wave channels support, and what effect did they have?
column2: 12.5%, 25%, 50%, and 75% duty cycles, each producing a distinct harmonic profile/timbre—e.g., 12.5% gave a thin, nasal sound—allowing composers to differentiate instrument voices.

column1: What do the ADSR envelope generator stages control in a chip like the Commodore 64 SID, and what gave them their characteristic sound?
column2: ADSR controls Attack, Decay, Sustain, and Release phases of a sound's amplitude over time; the SID's capacitor charge curves produced exponential (rather than linear) slopes, giving percussive sounds their punch and sustained notes their gradual fade.
